name: Yazid ibn Muawiyah
line: The son of Muawiyah, whose short reign saw the tragedy of Karbala.
story: Named heir by his father, he became caliph in 680. His reign saw the killing of Husayn ibn Ali and his family at Karbala, the sack of Madinah after the Battle of al-Harra in 683, and the siege of Makkah against Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. He died suddenly that same year.
note: Most Sunni scholars condemn the killing of Husayn and the sack of Madinah; they differ over how far Yazid himself ordered them, and over whether he may be cursed by name.
title: Caliph

name: Muawiyah ibn Yazid
line: A young caliph who ruled a few months and is said to have refused to name an heir.
story: He came to power as a sickly young man while much of the empire followed Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr in Makkah. Chroniclers report that he declined to pass the caliphate to a relative and died within months.
title: Caliph

name: Marwan ibn al-Hakam
line: An elder of the Umayyad clan who saved its rule in Syria.
story: With the caliphate split, Syrian tribes chose him as caliph. His victory at Marj Rahit in 684 kept Syria for the Umayyads, and he began the Marwanid line that ruled until 750. He died within a year, naming his son Abd al-Malik.
note: Born in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime; most scholars count him among the Tabi'un rather than the Companions.
title: Caliph

name: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan
role: Builder of the Dome of the Rock
line: The caliph who reunited the empire, built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic its language.
story: He ended the second civil war when Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr was killed in Makkah in 692. He raised the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, minted the first coins carrying only Quranic words, and made Arabic the language of government.
legacy: The Dome of the Rock still stands as the oldest surviving great monument of Islam.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik
line: Under him Muslim rule reached Spain, Sindh and Central Asia.
story: His generals Tariq ibn Ziyad, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim and Qutayba ibn Muslim pushed the empire from the Atlantic to the Indus. He built the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus and had the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah rebuilt and enlarged.
title: Caliph

name: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik
line: The caliph who sent the great siege against Constantinople and named Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as heir.
story: He launched the land and sea siege of Constantinople in 717 under his brother Maslamah. On his deathbed, on the advice of the scholar Raja ibn Haywa, he named his cousin Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as his successor.
title: Caliph

name: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
line: A great-grandson of Umar ibn al-Khattab whose short, just reign is remembered as a return to the Rashidun way.
story: He gave up his family's luxuries, returned seized property, cut unjust taxes and sent preachers rather than armies. He asked scholars to write down the Prophet's ﷺ hadith before they were lost. He died after about two and a half years.
legacy: Many scholars call him the fifth rightly guided caliph.
lesson: Power can be carried as a trust rather than a prize.
title: Caliph

name: Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik
line: A caliph whose reign undid many of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's reforms.
story: He crushed the revolt of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in Iraq and reversed several of his predecessor's tax reforms. Chroniclers remember him more for court pleasures than for statecraft.
title: Caliph

name: Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik
line: A careful, long-reigning caliph whose rule marked the furthest reach of the Umayyad state.
story: From his palace at Rusafa he ruled for nineteen years. His armies were checked at Tours in 732, and a great Berber revolt broke out in North Africa in 740. He was known as frugal and hard-working.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Walid ibn Yazid
line: A poet-caliph whose open misconduct turned his own family against him.
story: Chroniclers describe him as a gifted poet who mocked religion and neglected rule. Within about a year his cousin Yazid rose against him and he was killed in 744, opening the third civil war.
title: Caliph

name: Yazid ibn al-Walid
line: He overthrew al-Walid II, promised reform, and died months later.
story: He took power with the support of reformers and promised to rule justly and not hoard wealth. He died of illness within six months, leaving the dynasty divided.
title: Caliph

name: Ibrahim ibn al-Walid
line: A brief caliph, never widely obeyed, who gave way to Marwan II.
story: Named after his brother Yazid III, he was not accepted by much of the empire. When Marwan ibn Muhammad marched on Damascus he fled, and later submitted to him.
title: Caliph

name: Marwan ibn Muhammad
line: A tough soldier-caliph who lost the empire to the Abbasid revolution.
story: A veteran of the Caucasus wars, he ruled from Harran and spent his reign fighting rebels. The Abbasid armies from Khurasan defeated him at the Great Zab in 750, and he was killed in Egypt that same year.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Saffah
line: The first Abbasid caliph, from the family of the Prophet's ﷺ uncle al-Abbas.
story: Proclaimed caliph at Kufa in 749, he saw his forces destroy the Umayyad army at the Great Zab in 750. Many Umayyad princes were hunted down and killed. He died of smallpox four years later.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mansur
line: The stern caliph who built Baghdad, the Round City, in 762.
story: He secured the new dynasty, crushing rivals and revolts. He chose a site on the Tigris and built the Round City of Baghdad. He pressed Abu Hanifa to become judge; Abu Hanifa refused and was imprisoned. Al-Mansur died on his way to Hajj.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mahdi
line: A generous caliph who enlarged the Sacred Mosque in Makkah.
story: He released many prisoners of his father's reign and spent freely. He greatly expanded the Masjid al-Haram and pursued groups he accused of heresy.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Hadi
line: A short-lived caliph who died after a single year.
story: He crushed an Alid uprising at Fakhkh near Makkah in 786. He tried to set aside his brother Harun as heir but died suddenly the same year.
title: Caliph

name: Harun al-Rashid
line: The caliph of the Thousand and One Nights, when Baghdad was the richest city on earth.
story: He went on Hajj many times and led campaigns against Byzantium. His court gathered scholars, poets and physicians, and his wife Zubaydah built the pilgrim road to Makkah. He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne and died at Tus in 809.
legacy: His reign became the picture of the golden age in Muslim and world memory.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Amin
line: Harun's son, killed in a civil war with his brother al-Mamun.
story: Harun divided the succession between his sons. Al-Amin tried to cut his brother out, war followed, and Baghdad was besieged for a year. He was killed when the city fell in 813.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mamun
role: Patron of the House of Wisdom
line: A scholar-caliph who sponsored translation and science, and also began the Mihna.
story: He gathered scholars in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, where Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated and al-Khwarizmi wrote on algebra. In 833 he began the Mihna, forcing scholars to say the Quran was created; Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused.
note: The Mihna (inquisition) lasted under three caliphs and ended under al-Mutawakkil.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutasim
line: The caliph of the Turkish guard, remembered for answering a woman's cry at Amorium.
story: He built an army of Turkish slave-soldiers and moved the capital to Samarra in 836. In 838 he sacked Amorium; later stories say he marched after a captive Muslim woman cried out 'Wa Mutasimah!' He continued the Mihna and Ahmad ibn Hanbal was flogged.
note: The story of the woman's cry is popular but its details are not firmly established.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Wathiq
line: A curious caliph who is said to have sent an expedition to find the wall of Dhul-Qarnayn.
story: He kept the Mihna in force. Geographers report that he sent Sallam the Interpreter to Central Asia to look for the barrier against Yajuj and Majuj, and that Sallam brought back a description of an iron wall.
note: Sallam's journey is reported by the geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih; where he really went is debated.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutawakkil
line: He ended the Mihna and built the Great Mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret.
story: He stopped the persecution of scholars over the createdness of the Quran and honoured Ahmad ibn Hanbal. He built the Great Mosque of Samarra. In 861 he was murdered by Turkish officers, opening years of chaos.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muntasir
line: He came to power after his father's murder and died within six months.
story: Many chroniclers say he was involved in the plot against al-Mutawakkil. He died months later, and the Turkish commanders chose the next caliphs.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustain
line: A caliph raised and removed by the Turkish generals.
story: During the 'Anarchy at Samarra' he fled to Baghdad, was besieged, abdicated in 866 and was killed soon after.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutazz
line: A young caliph who could not pay the army and was deposed by it.
story: He tried to break the power of the Turkish officers but ran out of money to pay them. They forced him to abdicate in 869 and he died in captivity days later.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muhtadi
line: A devout caliph who tried to restore justice and was killed for it.
story: He lived simply, fasted often and sat in person to hear complaints, and chroniclers compared him to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. When he moved against the Turkish commanders they killed him after less than a year.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutamid
line: A long-reigning caliph whose brother al-Muwaffaq held the real power.
story: His brother led the armies and finally crushed the great Zanj slave revolt in southern Iraq in 883. In these years Egypt slipped away under Ahmad ibn Tulun. Near the end of his reign the court returned to Baghdad.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutadid
line: An energetic caliph who restored order and treasury after the years of chaos.
story: Son of al-Muwaffaq, he ruled firmly from Baghdad, balanced the budget and won back provinces. His reign was the last strong revival before the Buyids.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muktafi
line: He fought the Qarmatians and brought Egypt back under Baghdad.
story: His armies defeated Qarmatian raiders in Syria and in 905 ended the Tulunid dynasty, returning Egypt to direct Abbasid rule. He died young.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muqtadir
line: A boy-caliph whose long reign drained the treasury while the Qarmatians stole the Black Stone.
story: He took the throne at thirteen and was ruled by viziers and courtiers. His envoy Ibn Fadlan travelled to the Volga in 921. In 930 the Qarmatians raided Makkah and carried off the Black Stone. He was killed in battle in 932.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Qahir
line: A harsh caliph who was blinded and deposed.
story: He ruled with suspicion and cruelty and was overthrown and blinded in 934. Chroniclers say he later lived in poverty in Baghdad.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Radi
line: The caliph who handed real power to a military 'chief amir'.
story: In 936 he created the post of amir al-umara, giving a general control of the army and treasury. He is often called the last caliph to hold real authority before the Buyids.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muttaqi
line: A caliph caught between warlords, blinded and deposed.
story: He fled Baghdad to seek help from the Hamdanids, was tricked into returning, and was blinded and deposed in 944.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustakfi
line: In his time the Buyids entered Baghdad and took over the caliphate's power.
story: The Buyid Ahmad (Muizz al-Dawla) entered Baghdad in 945. The next year he had al-Mustakfi blinded and replaced. From then the caliphs reigned but did not rule.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muti
line: A caliph under Buyid control, in whose time the Black Stone came back to Makkah.
story: For almost thirty years he held only a ceremonial role. In 951 the Qarmatians returned the Black Stone to the Kaaba. He abdicated after a stroke.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Tai
line: A ceremonial caliph deposed by a Buyid amir.
story: He served under the Buyids, including Adud al-Dawla, and was deposed by Baha al-Dawla in 991.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Qadir
line: A long-reigning caliph who restored the caliph's role as defender of Sunni belief.
story: Without armies of his own, he used religious authority. He issued the 'Qadiri creed', a public statement of Sunni belief, and recognised Mahmud of Ghazna as sultan.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Qaim
line: In his reign Tughril Beg ended Buyid control and the Seljuks became the caliph's swords.
story: Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in 1055. In 1058 the rebel al-Basasiri briefly had the Friday sermon read for the Fatimids in Baghdad and al-Qaim was exiled for a year, until Tughril restored him.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muqtadi
line: A caliph of the Seljuk heyday under Malik Shah and Nizam al-Mulk.
story: His time saw the Nizamiyya madrasa flourish in Baghdad. He married a daughter of Malik Shah, but relations with the sultan were often tense.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustazhir
line: The caliph in Baghdad when the Crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099.
story: Refugees from Syria came to Baghdad pleading for help, but divided Seljuk princes sent little. Al-Ghazali wrote a book against the Batini sect for him, known as al-Mustazhiri.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustarshid
line: A caliph who led his own army against the Seljuks and was killed.
story: He tried to win back real power and took the field himself. He was captured by Sultan Masud in 1135 and murdered in captivity by Assassins.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Rashid
line: A caliph deposed within a year by the Seljuk sultan.
story: He tried to avenge his father but was deposed in 1136 and later killed by Assassins.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muqtafi
line: He won the caliphate real independence in Iraq again as Seljuk power faded.
story: He held Baghdad against a Seljuk siege in 1157 and ruled Iraq directly, the first caliph in two centuries to do so.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustanjid
line: A caliph known for lowering taxes and ruling Iraq firmly.
story: He continued his father's independent rule of Iraq and is remembered for justice in taxation.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustadi
line: In his reign Salah al-Din ended the Fatimids and had the sermon read again for Baghdad.
story: In 1171 Salah al-Din restored the Abbasid name in the Friday sermon in Egypt, ending two centuries of Fatimid rule there.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Nasir li-Din Allah
line: A clever caliph who ruled 45 years and tried to rebuild the caliph's prestige.
story: He used the futuwwa brotherhoods and Sufi orders to bind princes to him. He clashed with the Khwarazm Shah, who once marched on Baghdad. His reign was the longest of any Abbasid caliph.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Zahir
line: A just caliph who reigned only nine months.
story: He came to the throne in his fifties, lowered taxes and freed prisoners, and chroniclers praised his fairness. He died within the year.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustansir
line: He founded the Mustansiriyya, a college teaching all four Sunni schools of law.
story: The Mustansiriyya madrasa opened in Baghdad in 1233 with teachers of the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools. Its building still stands. Mongol armies were already raiding the east.
legacy: The Mustansiriyya is one of the oldest surviving university buildings in the world.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustasim
line: The last caliph of Baghdad, killed by Hulagu when the city fell in 1258.
story: Badly advised and slow to act, he refused Hulagu's demands without preparing the city. The Mongols took Baghdad in February 1258, killed vast numbers and destroyed its libraries. The caliph was put to death; tradition says rolled in a carpet and trampled.
lesson: Wealth and a great name do not protect a people that will not prepare.
note: The carpet detail comes from later chroniclers; accounts of his death vary.
title: Caliph

name: Abd al-Rahman I
line: An Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid massacre and founded a new state in al-Andalus.
story: He fled Syria as a young man, crossed North Africa in hiding and landed in Spain in 755. He took Cordoba in 756 and began its Great Mosque in 785. Even his enemy al-Mansur called him 'the Falcon of Quraysh'.
title: Emir

name: Hisham I
line: A devout emir under whom the Maliki school took root in al-Andalus.
story: He completed the first Great Mosque of Cordoba and favoured students of Imam Malik, so the Maliki school became the law of al-Andalus.
title: Emir

name: Al-Hakam I
line: A hard emir who crushed the revolt of the Cordoba suburb in 818.
story: Scholars and townsfolk rose against his taxes and harshness in 818. He crushed the revolt and exiled thousands, many of whom settled in Fez and Alexandria.
title: Emir

name: Abd al-Rahman II
line: A cultured emir who brought Baghdad's fashions and learning to Cordoba.
story: He welcomed the musician Ziryab from Baghdad, who changed Andalusi music, dress and dining. He enlarged the Great Mosque and beat off a Viking attack on Seville in 844.
title: Emir

name: Muhammad I of Cordoba
line: His long reign saw the start of the great revolt of Umar ibn Hafsun.
story: He faced rebels in the frontier lands and, from 880, the rising of Umar ibn Hafsun in the southern mountains, which would trouble Cordoba for almost fifty years.
title: Emir

name: Al-Mundhir
line: A brief emir who died while besieging the rebel Ibn Hafsun.
story: He reigned two years and died during the siege of Bobastro.
title: Emir

name: Abdallah ibn Muhammad
line: An emir whose state shrank almost to the city of Cordoba itself.
story: Revolts by Arabs, Berbers and converts broke the emirate into pieces during his reign. He left the throne to his grandson Abd al-Rahman.
title: Emir

name: Abd al-Rahman III
line: He reunited al-Andalus and in 929 declared himself caliph, making Cordoba a rival to Baghdad and Cairo.
story: Taking a broken emirate at twenty-one, he spent decades restoring it. In 929 he took the title caliph. He built the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra, and Cordoba became the largest and most learned city in Europe.
legacy: Cordoba under him drew scholars, physicians and envoys from across Europe and the Muslim world.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Hakam II
line: A book-loving caliph whose library was said to hold 400,000 volumes.
story: He sent agents across the Muslim world to buy books and built the splendid mihrab of the Great Mosque of Cordoba. Peace with the Christian kingdoms let learning flourish.
note: The 400,000 figure comes from medieval writers and may be exaggerated.
title: Caliph

name: Hisham II
line: A child caliph whose power was held by his chamberlain al-Mansur.
story: He came to the throne aged about ten and never ruled in person. After al-Mansur's family fell in 1009, civil war broke out and the caliphate began to collapse.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mansur ibn Abi Amir
line: The chamberlain who ruled al-Andalus for Hisham II and led more than fifty campaigns.
story: Rising from a minor official, he took control of the state and kept the young caliph out of sight. He raided the Christian north again and again, reaching Santiago de Compostela in 997. He died on campaign in 1002.
note: He ruled as regent, never as caliph. Christians called him Almanzor.
title: Hajib (regent)

name: Hisham III
line: The last Umayyad caliph; after him al-Andalus split into small 'taifa' kingdoms.
story: The notables of Cordoba deposed him in 1031 and abolished the caliphate. Al-Andalus broke into more than twenty rival kingdoms, which Christian kings soon played against each other.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mutamid ibn Abbad
line: The poet-king of Seville who called in the Almoravids and died in their prison.
story: Pressed for tribute by Alfonso VI, he invited Yusuf ibn Tashfin, reportedly saying he would rather herd camels in Africa than pigs in Castile. The Almoravids later removed him and exiled him to Aghmat, where he wrote moving poems.
note: He ruled the taifa of Seville, which has no separate polity entry. The camel saying is reported by chroniclers.
title: King

name: Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah
line: The founder of the Fatimid caliphate in North Africa.
story: Isma'ili missionaries won over the Kutama Berbers and overthrew the Aghlabids. In 909 he was proclaimed caliph and imam, and he built a new capital, Mahdia, on the Tunisian coast.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Muizz li-Din Allah
line: The Fatimid caliph whose general conquered Egypt and founded Cairo and al-Azhar.
story: His general Jawhar took Egypt in 969 and laid out a new city, al-Qahira. The al-Azhar mosque opened in 972, and al-Muizz moved his court to Cairo in 973.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Aziz Billah
line: Under him Fatimid power reached into Syria and al-Azhar became a teaching mosque.
story: He extended Fatimid rule over much of Syria and employed Christians and Jews in high office. Al-Azhar began formal teaching in his reign.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
line: An erratic Fatimid caliph who destroyed the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and then vanished.
story: He issued strange and harsh decrees, persecuted Christians and Jews, and in 1009 ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem torn down. He also founded the House of Knowledge in Cairo. In 1021 he rode into the hills and was never seen again.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief. The Druze, who broke away in his time, revere him.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Mustansir Billah
line: His near sixty-year reign saw great famine in Egypt and a split that divided the Isma'ilis.
story: In 1059 his name was briefly read in the Friday sermon in Baghdad. A terrible famine struck Egypt in the 1060s. After his death a succession quarrel split the Isma'ilis, giving rise to the Nizari 'Assassins'.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief.
title: Caliph

name: Al-Adid
line: The last Fatimid caliph, a young man whose vizier Salah al-Din ended the dynasty.
story: He named Shirkuh and then Salah al-Din as his viziers. In 1171, as he lay dying, Salah al-Din had the Friday sermon read for the Abbasid caliph, closing two centuries of Fatimid rule.
note: The Fatimids were Isma'ili Shi'i imams who claimed descent from Fatimah; many Sunni historians disputed that lineage, and their doctrine differs from both Sunni and Twelver Shi'i belief.
title: Caliph

name: Tughril Beg
line: A Turkish chief from the steppe who freed the caliph from the Buyids and was named sultan.
story: With his brother Chaghri he beat the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and won Iran. In 1055 he entered Baghdad as protector of the Abbasid caliph, who gave him the title 'Sultan of East and West'.
title: Sultan

name: Alp Arslan
line: The Seljuk sultan who defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor at Manzikert in 1071.
story: With a smaller army he routed Romanos IV at Manzikert, opening Anatolia to the Turks. He treated the captured emperor with honour and freed him. He was stabbed by a prisoner a year later.
title: Sultan

name: Malik Shah I
line: Under him the Seljuk empire reached from Central Asia to the Mediterranean.
story: Guided by his vizier Nizam al-Mulk, he ruled a vast, settled empire from Isfahan. He sponsored a new solar calendar, worked out by Umar Khayyam and others. He died weeks after Nizam al-Mulk was murdered, and the empire split.
title: Sultan

name: Nizam al-Mulk
line: The Persian vizier who ran the Seljuk empire and founded the Nizamiyya colleges.
story: For nearly thirty years he governed for Alp Arslan and Malik Shah. He founded the Nizamiyya madrasas in Baghdad and other cities, where al-Ghazali taught, and wrote a book of advice on government. He was murdered in 1092, reportedly by an Assassin.
legacy: His madrasas became a model for Sunni higher learning for centuries.
title: Vizier

name: Ahmad Sanjar
line: The last great Seljuk sultan, who ruled the east from Merv for decades.
story: He governed Khurasan from 1097 and was supreme sultan from 1118. He was defeated by the Qara Khitai in 1141 and later captured by Oghuz tribesmen. His tomb still stands at Merv.
title: Sultan

name: Kilij Arslan I
role: Sultan who met the First Crusade
line: The Seljuk sultan of Anatolia who lost Nicaea to the First Crusade.
story: He underestimated the first Crusader army and lost his capital Nicaea in 1097 and the battle of Dorylaeum. In 1101 he destroyed a second wave of Crusaders.
title: Sultan

name: Kayqubad I
line: The sultan of Konya who built caravanserais across Anatolia and welcomed Rumi's family.
story: Under him the Seljuks of Rum were at their height. He built roads, inns and the port of Alanya. He welcomed the scholar Baha al-Din Walad, father of Jalal al-Din Rumi, to Konya.
title: Sultan

name: Imad al-Din Zengi
line: The ruler of Mosul whose capture of Edessa in 1144 was the first great Muslim victory over the Crusaders.
story: A hard Turkish commander, he joined Mosul and Aleppo. In 1144 he took Edessa, the first Crusader state, which prompted the Second Crusade. He was killed by one of his servants in 1146.
title: Atabeg

name: Nur al-Din Zengi
line: A pious ruler who united Syria and prepared the way for Salah al-Din.
story: He took Damascus in 1154, joined Syria and sent armies to Egypt. He built hospitals, madrasas and schools of hadith, and had a minbar carved for al-Aqsa, which Salah al-Din later installed. He was known for his simple life.
legacy: His hospital in Damascus and his minbar for al-Aqsa became symbols of his reign.
lesson: He worked for a victory he would not live to see.
title: Sultan

name: Shirkuh
line: Nur al-Din's general who won Egypt and became its vizier, with his nephew Salah al-Din at his side.
story: A Kurdish commander, he led three campaigns into Egypt to stop the Crusaders taking it. In 1169 he became vizier of the Fatimid caliph but died two months later, and Salah al-Din took his place.
title: Vizier

name: Salah al-Din
line: The Kurdish sultan who united Egypt and Syria, won at Hattin and took back Jerusalem in 1187.
story: Vizier of Egypt from 1169, he ended Fatimid rule in 1171 and became sultan. In July 1187 he destroyed the Crusader army at Hattin and entered Jerusalem without a massacre. He held off Richard I, made a truce in 1192 and died in Damascus, leaving almost no wealth.
legacy: Muslims and Europeans alike remembered him as a model of chivalry.
lesson: Strength and mercy can belong to the same man.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Adil
line: Salah al-Din's brother, who reunited the Ayyubid lands after family quarrels.
story: He served as his brother's right hand and negotiator with Richard I. After years of rivalry among Salah al-Din's sons he became sultan in 1200. Crusaders called him Saphadin.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Kamil
line: He defeated the Fifth Crusade, met Francis of Assisi, and controversially handed Jerusalem to Frederick II.
story: He beat back the Crusaders at Damietta in 1221 and received the friar Francis of Assisi in his camp. In 1229, to avoid war, he gave Jerusalem to Frederick II by treaty for ten years, which angered many Muslims.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Salih Ayyub
line: The Ayyubid sultan whose slave-soldiers, the Mamluks, would soon replace his dynasty.
story: He bought large numbers of Turkish slave-soldiers and housed them on the Nile island of Roda. He died in 1249 as Louis IX invaded Egypt; his wife Shajar al-Durr hid his death to keep the army together.
title: Sultan

name: Turan Shah
line: The heir who arrived in time to defeat Louis IX, then was killed by his father's Mamluks.
story: His army captured Louis IX at Fariskur in 1250. He soon quarrelled with the Mamluk officers, who killed him that May, ending Ayyubid rule in Egypt.
title: Sultan

name: Shajar al-Durr
line: A former slave who ruled Egypt as sultan for about eighty days and opened the Mamluk era.
story: She hid her husband's death to keep the army fighting Louis IX. After Turan Shah was killed, the Mamluks made her sultan, and coins were struck in her name. Under pressure from Baghdad she married the commander Aybak and gave up the throne. She was killed in 1257.
title: Sultana

name: Izz al-Din Aybak
line: The first Mamluk sultan, who married Shajar al-Durr.
story: He ruled with her for seven years and fought the Ayyubids of Syria. When he planned a second marriage, he was murdered in his bath in 1257.
title: Sultan

name: Qutuz
line: The sultan who stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260.
story: With the Mongols at Syria's gates after Baghdad's fall, he killed Hulagu's envoys and marched out. At Ain Jalut in September 1260 his army defeated the Mongols, saving Egypt. Weeks later he was killed by fellow officers including Baybars.
title: Sultan

name: Baybars
line: A Kipchak former slave who became the most powerful sultan of his age.
story: He fought at Ain Jalut, then took the throne. He brought an Abbasid prince to Cairo as caliph in 1261, built a fast postal system, and won back much of the coast from the Crusaders, taking Antioch in 1268. He died in Damascus.
title: Sultan

name: Qalawun
line: A sultan who beat the Mongols in 1281 and built Cairo's great hospital.
story: He defeated the Ilkhanid army at Homs in 1281 and took Tripoli in 1289. His complex in Cairo held a hospital open to all, rich or poor. His descendants ruled for most of a century.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Ashraf Khalil
line: The sultan who took Acre in 1291, ending the Crusader states.
story: He finished his father's plans and took Acre after a six-week siege in 1291. The last Crusader towns fell soon after. He was murdered by his own emirs in 1293.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Nasir Muhammad
role: Mamluk sultan of the golden years
line: A sultan who reigned three times and presided over Mamluk Cairo at its height.
story: Twice deposed as a boy, he took full power in 1310. His armies beat the Mongols at Marj al-Saffar in 1303, where Ibn Taymiyya fought. He filled Cairo with mosques, canals and palaces.
title: Sultan

name: Barquq
line: The first sultan of the Circassian Mamluks, who appointed Ibn Khaldun a judge in Cairo.
story: He seized the throne from Qalawun's line, lost it, and won it back in 1390. He made Ibn Khaldun the Maliki chief judge and built a great madrasa on Cairo's main street.
title: Sultan

name: Barsbay
line: A Mamluk sultan who conquered Cyprus and controlled the spice trade.
story: His fleet raided and then conquered Cyprus in 1426, capturing its king. He also made the spice trade through Egypt a state monopoly.
title: Sultan

name: Qaitbay
line: A long-reigning sultan who rebuilt the Prophet's Mosque after a fire and built the citadel of Alexandria.
story: He gave the Mamluk state its last long, stable reign. After lightning set the Prophet's Mosque ablaze in 1481 he had it rebuilt. His fort stands where the lighthouse of Alexandria once was.
title: Sultan

name: Qansuh al-Ghawri
role: Mamluk sultan killed at Marj Dabiq
line: One of the last Mamluk sultans, who died fighting the Ottomans in 1516.
story: He fought the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean after Vasco da Gama's voyage, without success. In 1516 he met Selim I at Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo, where Ottoman guns won and the old sultan died on the field.
title: Sultan

name: Tumanbay II
line: The last Mamluk sultan, hanged at a gate of Cairo by the Ottomans.
story: He tried to defend Cairo after al-Ghawri's death but lost at Ridaniyya in January 1517. He fought on, was betrayed and hanged at Bab Zuwayla in April 1517.
title: Sultan

name: Al-Mutawakkil III
line: The last of the Abbasid 'shadow caliphs' kept by the Mamluks in Cairo.
story: Since 1261 the Mamluks had kept Abbasid caliphs in Cairo with little power. After the Ottoman conquest he was taken to Istanbul, later returning to Cairo, where he died in 1543.
note: A later tradition says he handed the caliphate to Selim I; early sources do not clearly report this.
title: Caliph

name: Yusuf ibn Tashfin
line: The Almoravid leader who built Marrakesh and saved al-Andalus at the Battle of Zallaqa in 1086.
story: A Sanhaja Berber of the Almoravid movement, he took charge in the north and helped found Marrakesh. Called in by the taifa kings, he crushed Alfonso VI at Zallaqa in 1086. He later took over al-Andalus himself and died at a great age.
legacy: He took the title 'Commander of the Muslims' and left the caliph's title to Baghdad.
title: Emir

name: Ali ibn Yusuf
line: A pious Almoravid ruler who lost ground to the Almohads.
story: He ruled an empire from Spain to Senegal and favoured Maliki jurists. In his later years the Almohad movement rose in the Atlas Mountains.
title: Emir

name: Ibn Tumart
line: A Berber preacher who founded the Almohad movement and claimed to be the Mahdi.
story: He studied in the east and returned preaching strict tawhid and attacking the Almoravids. In 1121 his followers hailed him as the Mahdi, and he made his base at Tinmel in the High Atlas. He died before his movement won.
note: Most Sunni scholars rejected his claim to be the Mahdi.
title: Imam

name: Abd al-Mumin
line: Ibn Tumart's successor, who took Marrakesh and united North Africa from the Atlantic to Libya.
story: He took Marrakesh in 1147, ending the Almoravids, and pushed east to Tunisia by 1160. He took the title caliph and crossed into al-Andalus.
title: Caliph

name: Yaqub al-Mansur
line: The Almohad caliph who won at Alarcos and built the Koutoubia and Giralda towers.
story: He defeated Castile at Alarcos in 1195. He raised the minarets of the Koutoubia in Marrakesh and of Seville, now the Giralda. He employed Ibn Rushd as judge and doctor, exiled him for a time, then recalled him.
title: Caliph

name: Muhammad al-Nasir
line: The Almohad caliph whose defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 opened al-Andalus to conquest.
story: He crushed a revolt in Tunisia, then led a huge army into Spain. At Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 a united Christian army routed him, and within forty years most of al-Andalus was lost.
title: Caliph

name: Muhammad I of Granada
line: The founder of the kingdom of Granada, who began the Alhambra.
story: As Cordoba and Seville fell, he made Granada a refuge. He kept it alive by paying Castile tribute. He began the Alhambra, whose walls carry his motto, 'There is no victor but Allah'.
title: Sultan

name: Yusuf I of Granada
line: A Nasrid sultan who built much of the Alhambra and founded Granada's madrasa.
story: He built the Gate of Justice and Comares Palace in the Alhambra and opened the Yusufiyya madrasa in 1349. He was stabbed while praying in the mosque on Eid in 1354.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad V of Granada
role: Builder of the Court of the Lions
line: The sultan of Granada's golden age, who built the Court of the Lions.
story: Driven out in 1359, he returned in 1362 and ruled for thirty more years. His palace of the Lions is the Alhambra's most famous part. The scholar Ibn al-Khatib served as his vizier.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad XII
line: Boabdil, the last Muslim ruler in Spain, who handed Granada's keys to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
story: He fought his father and uncle for the throne while Castile and Aragon closed in. After a long siege he surrendered Granada on 2 January 1492, under a treaty promising Muslims their faith. He died in exile in Morocco.
note: The story that his mother scolded him as he looked back weeping is a later legend.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad al-Mustansir
line: The Hafsid ruler of Tunis who saw off the last Crusade of Louis IX.
story: He took the title caliph in 1253 after Baghdad's caliphate weakened. In 1270 Louis IX landed at Carthage, but the king died of disease in camp and the Crusade ended with a treaty.
title: Caliph

name: Abu Inan Faris
line: The Marinid sultan who had Ibn Battuta's travels written down.
story: He built the Bou Inania madrasas in Fez and Meknes. In 1355 he ordered the scholar Ibn Juzayy to record the travels of Ibn Battuta, giving the world the Rihla. He was strangled by his vizier in 1358.
title: Sultan

name: Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab
line: An Abbasid governor whose family ruled Ifriqiya as a near-independent dynasty.
story: Harun al-Rashid made him hereditary governor of Ifriqiya in exchange for tribute. He built the palace city of al-Abbasiyya near Kairouan.
title: Emir

name: Ziyadat Allah I
line: The Aghlabid emir who began the conquest of Sicily and rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
story: In 827 he sent a fleet to Sicily under the elderly judge Asad ibn al-Furat, beginning more than two centuries of Muslim rule there. In 836 he rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan much as it stands today.
title: Emir

name: Idris I
line: A descendant of Hasan ibn Ali who founded Morocco's first Muslim dynasty.
story: He escaped the Abbasids after a failed uprising near Makkah in 786 and reached the far Maghreb. The Awraba Berbers at Walila made him their imam in 788. He died in 791, reportedly poisoned by an Abbasid agent.
title: Imam

name: Idris II
line: The son of Idris I, born after his father's death, who made Fez his capital.
story: Raised by his father's freedman Rashid, he took power as a youth. He founded his part of Fez around 809, settling Arab refugees from Cordoba and Kairouan there. His shrine in Fez is still visited.
title: Imam

name: Ahmad ibn Tulun
line: A Turkish governor who made Egypt independent and built the mosque that bears his name.
story: Sent to Egypt by the Abbasids, he built his own army and treasury and added Syria to his rule. His great mosque of 879, with its spiral minaret, is the oldest mosque in Cairo in its original form.
note: He ruled Egypt as an independent governor under nominal Abbasid authority; the Tulunids have no separate polity entry.
title: Emir

name: Sayf al-Dawla
line: The Arab emir of Aleppo who fought Byzantium for twenty years and hosted al-Mutanabbi and al-Farabi.
story: He led yearly campaigns against the Byzantines on the frontier, winning and losing in turn. His court drew the poet al-Mutanabbi, who praised him in famous odes, and the philosopher al-Farabi.
note: The Hamdanids ruled Aleppo under nominal Abbasid authority; they have no separate polity entry.
title: Emir

name: Ismail ibn Ahmad
line: The Samanid emir who made Bukhara a capital of learning and Persian culture.
story: He defeated the Saffarids in 900 and ruled Khurasan and Transoxiana in the caliph's name. Bukhara grew into a centre of scholarship where Persian literature revived. His brick mausoleum in Bukhara still stands.
title: Emir

name: Adud al-Dawla
line: The greatest Buyid ruler, who governed Iraq and Iran and built a famous hospital in Baghdad.
story: From Shiraz he united the Buyid lands and in 978 took Baghdad. He repaired the city, built canals and dams, and founded the Adudi hospital. He took the old Persian title Shahanshah.
note: The Buyids were Shi'i but kept the Sunni Abbasid caliphs in place as figureheads.
title: Emir

name: Sebuktigin
line: A Turkish slave-soldier who founded the Ghaznavid dynasty at Ghazni.
story: Once a slave of the Samanids, he became ruler of Ghazni in 977 and pushed into the Punjab. His son Mahmud built an empire on his foundations.
title: Emir

name: Mahmud of Ghazna
line: A warrior-king, among the first to be called 'Sultan', who raided deep into India and gathered great scholars.
story: He led many campaigns into India, including the sack of Somnath in 1025, and ruled from Iran to the Punjab. His court held al-Biruni and received the poet Firdawsi's Shahnama. The caliph al-Qadir honoured him for supporting Sunni Islam.
note: His Indian raids are remembered very differently in Muslim and Hindu memory.
title: Sultan

name: Qutb al-Din Aibak
line: A former slave who became the first Sultan of Delhi and began the Qutb Minar.
story: A general of Muhammad of Ghor, he ruled the conquered lands in north India after his master's death in 1206. He began the Quwwat al-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar, and died in a polo accident in Lahore.
title: Sultan

name: Iltutmish
line: The real founder of the Delhi Sultanate, recognised by the Abbasid caliph.
story: Another former slave, he kept north India safe while Genghis Khan ravaged Central Asia. He completed the Qutb Minar and in 1229 received robes of investiture from the caliph in Baghdad.
title: Sultan

name: Razia Sultana
line: The only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate.
story: Her father Iltutmish chose her over her brothers. She held court unveiled and rode at the head of her army, which offended many nobles. They rose against her, and she was killed in 1240.
title: Sultana

name: Ghiyath al-Din Balban
line: A strict sultan who restored order and held off the Mongols.
story: He broke the power of rival nobles, insisted on stern court ceremony and guarded the north-west frontier against the Mongols.
title: Sultan

name: Alauddin Khalji
line: A ruthless sultan who repelled repeated Mongol invasions of India.
story: He beat back several large Mongol armies between 1297 and 1306, saving north India from the fate of Iran. He fixed market prices and sent his general Malik Kafur deep into the south.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad bin Tughluq
line: A learned but unpredictable sultan whose bold schemes often failed.
story: He moved the capital to Daulatabad and back, and issued copper tokens that were soon forged everywhere. The traveller Ibn Battuta served as a judge at his court and described both his generosity and his cruelty.
title: Sultan

name: Firuz Shah Tughluq
line: A mild sultan remembered for canals, hospitals and new towns.
story: He dug canals, founded hospitals and towns and repaired old monuments. He ruled more gently than his cousin, though the empire shrank.
title: Sultan

name: Ibrahim Lodi
line: The last Sultan of Delhi, killed by Babur's army at Panipat in 1526.
story: His quarrels with his own nobles led some to invite Babur from Kabul. At Panipat in 1526 Babur's guns and horse archers beat his larger army, and he died on the field.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad II of Khwarazm
line: The proud Khwarazm Shah whose killing of Mongol envoys brought Genghis Khan west.
story: He built a huge empire from Central Asia to Iran and quarrelled even with the caliph. In 1218 his governor at Otrar killed a Mongol trade caravan, and he then killed an envoy. Genghis Khan invaded, and Muhammad fled, dying on a Caspian island.
lesson: One arrogant act can bring ruin on millions.
title: Shah

name: Jalal al-Din Mangburni
role: Khwarazmian prince who fought the Mongols
line: Muhammad II's brave son, who kept fighting the Mongols for eleven years.
story: He beat a Mongol army at Parwan in 1221, then, defeated on the Indus, famously leapt his horse into the river and escaped. He roamed Iran and the Caucasus fighting until he was killed in Kurdistan in 1231.
title: Shah

name: Berke Khan
line: A grandson of Genghis Khan and the first Mongol ruler to become Muslim.
story: He accepted Islam before taking the throne, reportedly through a Sufi teacher from Bukhara. Angered by Hulagu's sack of Baghdad, he allied with the Mamluk sultan Baybars and went to war with Hulagu in 1262.
legacy: His war with Hulagu split the Mongol world and helped protect Mamluk Egypt.
title: Khan

name: Ozbeg Khan
role: Khan who made the Golden Horde Muslim
line: The khan under whom Islam became the faith of the Golden Horde.
story: He made Islam the state religion of the Golden Horde and built mosques in his capital Sarai. Ibn Battuta visited his camp and described his court.
title: Khan

name: Ghazan
line: The Ilkhan who embraced Islam in 1295, bringing the Mongols of Iran into the faith.
story: A grandson of Hulagu's line, he became Muslim and took the name Mahmud. With his vizier Rashid al-Din he reformed taxes and sponsored a world history. Yet he still invaded Mamluk Syria, losing at Marj al-Saffar in 1303.
note: Ibn Taymiyya's well-known rulings on fighting Mongols who claimed Islam date from Ghazan's invasions.
title: Khan

name: Oljeitu
line: Ghazan's brother, who built the new capital Sultaniyya and its giant domed tomb.
story: Baptised as a child, he later became Muslim and moved between Sunni and Shi'i views. He built Sultaniyya, whose huge brick dome still stands.
title: Khan

name: Timur
line: A Turco-Mongol conqueror who called himself a Muslim yet massacred Muslim cities from Delhi to Damascus.
story: From Samarkand he conquered Iran, Iraq and Central Asia, sacked Delhi in 1398 and Baghdad and Damascus in 1401, and captured the Ottoman sultan at Ankara in 1402. His armies left towers of skulls at Isfahan and elsewhere. He met Ibn Khaldun outside Damascus. He died marching on China.
lesson: Fine mosques in one city do not wash away the blood of others.
note: Chroniclers report massacres of tens of thousands; exact numbers are uncertain.
title: Emir

name: Shah Rukh
line: Timur's son, who turned from conquest to scholarship and building.
story: He held most of his father's empire from Herat. His wife Gawhar Shad built a great mosque at Mashhad, and Herat became a centre of painting and learning.
title: Sultan

name: Ulugh Beg
line: Timur's grandson, a ruler and astronomer whose star tables were the best of their age.
story: As governor of Samarkand from 1409 he built a madrasa and a great observatory, where he and his team charted over a thousand stars. He ruled as sultan for only two years before his own son had him killed.
title: Sultan

name: Babur
line: A Timurid prince from Central Asia who founded the Mughal Empire at Panipat in 1526.
story: Driven from Samarkand, he made Kabul his base. In 1526 he defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and took Delhi and Agra. His memoir, the Baburnama, is one of the great autobiographies. He was buried in Kabul.
title: Emperor

name: Humayun
line: Babur's son, who lost his empire, lived in exile in Persia and won it back.
story: Defeated by the Afghan Sher Shah Suri in 1540, he fled to Safavid Persia. He returned and retook Delhi in 1555, but died months later after falling on his library stairs. His tomb in Delhi inspired the Taj Mahal.
title: Emperor

name: Akbar
line: The emperor who built Mughal India into a world power and ruled a mainly Hindu land.
story: Crowned at thirteen, he expanded the empire across north India. He abolished the jizya on non-Muslims, held debates among religions and built Fatehpur Sikri. His court ideas, including the Din-i Ilahi, were opposed by scholars such as Ahmad Sirhindi.
note: Historians debate how far the Din-i Ilahi was a new religion or a court circle of loyalty.
title: Emperor

name: Jahangir
line: Akbar's son, a lover of art and nature, whose wife Nur Jahan held great power.
story: He kept the empire at peace, sponsored fine painting and wrote a frank memoir. He received the first English envoy, Thomas Roe, in 1615. His wife Nur Jahan issued orders and coins in her own name.
title: Emperor

name: Shah Jahan
line: The Mughal emperor who built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
story: His reign was the high point of Mughal building: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid of Delhi. When he fell ill in 1657 his sons fought for the throne, and Aurangzeb kept him confined in Agra Fort until his death in 1666.
title: Emperor

name: Aurangzeb
line: The emperor who ruled the Mughal Empire at its largest and sponsored the Fatawa Alamgiri.
story: Known as Alamgir, he lived simply, copied Qurans and sewed caps to earn his keep, and had scholars compile the Fatawa Alamgiri of Hanafi law. He reimposed the jizya in 1679 and spent his last decades at war in the Deccan.
note: His legacy is sharply debated: some praise his piety, others blame his policies for weakening the empire.
title: Emperor

name: Bahadur Shah II
line: The poet-emperor whose reign ended the Mughal line after the uprising of 1857.
story: By his time he ruled little beyond Delhi's Red Fort. In 1857 rebel soldiers proclaimed him leader of the uprising against the East India Company. After its defeat the British exiled him to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.
title: Emperor

name: Shah Ismail I
line: The young founder of Safavid Iran, who made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion.
story: Leader of a Sufi order at fourteen, he took Tabriz in 1501 and was crowned shah. He imposed Twelver Shi'ism on Iran, often by force. Selim I defeated him at Chaldiran in 1514.
legacy: The Shi'i identity of modern Iran dates largely from his reign.
title: Shah

name: Tahmasp I
line: The long-reigning Safavid shah who sheltered the exiled Humayun.
story: He survived Ottoman invasions, made peace at Amasya in 1555 and moved his capital to Qazvin. He gave refuge to the Mughal Humayun and helped him regain India.
title: Shah

name: Shah Abbas I
line: The Safavid shah who made Isfahan one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
story: He rebuilt the army, won back land from the Ottomans and Uzbeks, and took Hormuz from the Portuguese in 1622. He moved the capital to Isfahan and built its great square and mosques.
title: Shah

name: Nader Shah
line: A soldier who ended the Safavids, sacked Delhi and tried to reconcile Sunni and Shi'i Islam.
story: He drove out Afghan and Ottoman invaders, then made himself shah in 1736, founding the Afsharid dynasty. In 1739 he sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. He tried to have Ja'fari Shi'ism accepted as a fifth school of law. He was murdered by his officers.
note: He founded the Afsharid dynasty after the Safavids; it has no separate polity entry.
title: Shah

name: Fath-Ali Shah Qajar
line: A Qajar shah under whom Iran lost the Caucasus to Russia.
story: His long-bearded portraits became famous. Two wars with Russia ended in the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828), giving up Muslim lands in the Caucasus.
title: Shah

name: Sundiata Keita
line: The 'Lion King' of Mali, whose victory at Kirina founded the Mali Empire.
story: Oral epics tell of a lame boy who rose to defeat the sorcerer-king Sumanguru at Kirina around 1235. He united the Mande peoples into an empire that grew rich on gold.
note: Most of what we know comes from the oral Epic of Sundiata; traditions differ on whether he was Muslim.
title: Mansa

name: Mansa Musa
line: The king of Mali whose Hajj in 1324 spread so much gold that prices fell in Cairo.
story: He crossed the Sahara to Makkah with thousands of followers and great loads of gold. He brought back scholars and the architect al-Sahili, and built the Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu, which grew into a city of learning.
legacy: European maps soon showed him on his throne holding a nugget of gold.
note: The dates of his reign are uncertain; some sources give 1307–1332.
title: Mansa

name: Mansa Sulayman
line: Mansa Musa's brother, whose court Ibn Battuta visited.
story: Ibn Battuta stayed in Mali in 1352–1353 and described its safety, its Friday prayers and the king's audiences.
title: Mansa

name: Sunni Ali
line: A warrior-king who built the Songhai Empire and took Timbuktu.
story: He took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenne after a long siege, building the largest empire in West Africa. He treated Timbuktu's scholars harshly, and many questioned the sincerity of his Islam.
title: King

name: Askia Muhammad I
line: The Songhai emperor who ruled by Islamic law and made Timbuktu a capital of scholarship.
story: He took power from Sunni Ali's son, then made Hajj in 1496–1497, where the Abbasid caliph in Cairo named him his deputy in West Africa. He sought advice from the scholar al-Maghili. His sons deposed him in old age.
title: Askia

name: Idris Alooma
line: A ruler of Bornu who used firearms, made Hajj and ruled by Islamic law.
story: He bought muskets and Turkish instructors, built mosques of brick and appointed judges. His imam Ahmad ibn Furtu wrote a chronicle of his wars.
note: Dates are uncertain; some historians give 1571–1603.
title: Mai

name: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
line: The imam of Adal who conquered much of Christian Ethiopia before being killed in battle.
story: From Harar he led the Adal Sultanate against Ethiopia, winning at Shimbra Kure in 1529. Portuguese soldiers came to Ethiopia's aid, and he was killed at Wayna Daga in 1543.
note: A painful chapter between Muslims and the Christian land that had sheltered the first emigrants; both sides remember it differently.
title: Imam

name: Tunka Manin
line: A non-Muslim king of Ghana whose ministers and treasurers were Muslims.
story: The geographer al-Bakri, writing in 1068, describes his capital as two towns, one with twelve mosques for Muslim traders. The king kept his own religion but trusted Muslim officials.
tie: Ghana shows how Islam first reached West Africa through trade and trust, not conquest.
title: King

name: Malik al-Salih
line: The first Muslim ruler of Samudra Pasai in Sumatra, whose gravestone is dated 1297.
story: Local chronicles say he accepted Islam and took the name Malik al-Salih. His port became an early centre of Islam in Southeast Asia, later visited by Ibn Battuta.
note: Pasai lay in north Sumatra, the later land of Aceh. The start of his reign is traditional.
title: Sultan

name: Iskandar Muda
line: The sultan under whom Aceh became the strongest Muslim state in the Malay world.
story: He built a powerful fleet, controlled the pepper trade and fought the Portuguese at Malacca, losing a great siege in 1629. His court welcomed scholars, and Aceh became known as 'the Veranda of Makkah'.
title: Sultan

name: Muhammad Bello
line: The scholar-son of Usman dan Fodio, who built the Sokoto Caliphate's towns and schools.
story: He took over from his father in 1817 as Commander of the Faithful. He founded Sokoto as a city, wrote dozens of books, including a history of the jihad, and received the British explorer Hugh Clapperton.
title: Caliph

name: Osman I
line: A Turkish frontier chief in Anatolia whose small state grew into the Ottoman Empire.
story: He led a band of warriors on the Byzantine border near Sogut. Later tradition tells of his dream of a great tree growing from his chest and shading the world. He won lands from Byzantium and his son took Bursa as he died.
note: The founding date of 1299 is traditional; early Ottoman history is known mostly from later sources.
title: Sultan

name: Orhan
line: Osman's son, who took Bursa and Nicaea and crossed into Europe.
story: He made Bursa his capital in 1326, took Nicaea in 1331 and founded the first Ottoman madrasa there. In 1354 his forces settled at Gallipoli, the first Ottoman foothold in Europe.
title: Sultan

name: Murad I
line: The sultan who moved the capital to Edirne and was killed at Kosovo.
story: He took Adrianople, renamed Edirne, and made it his capital. He organised the Janissary corps. He won the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 but was stabbed in his tent by a Serbian knight.
title: Sultan

name: Bayezid I
line: A lightning-fast sultan who crushed a Crusade at Nicopolis but was captured by Timur.
story: He destroyed a great Crusader army at Nicopolis in 1396 and besieged Constantinople. He built Bursa's Grand Mosque. In 1402 Timur defeated and captured him at Ankara, and he died in captivity.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed I
line: The son of Bayezid who reunited the empire after eleven years of civil war.
story: After Ankara, Bayezid's sons fought over the remains. Mehmed won in 1413 and rebuilt the state. He built the Green Mosque in Bursa.
title: Sultan

name: Murad II
line: A sultan who tried to retire, then returned to defeat a Crusade at Varna.
story: He handed the throne to his young son Mehmed in 1444, but when a Crusader army advanced he came back and won at Varna. He ruled again from 1446 until his death.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed II
line: The sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 at the age of twenty-one.
story: After a 53-day siege with giant cannon and ships hauled overland, his army took Constantinople on 29 May 1453. He prayed in Hagia Sophia, made the city his capital and invited its scattered people back. He went on to conquer Serbia, Bosnia and the Crimea's coast.
note: A hadith praising the commander and army that would conquer Constantinople is reported by Ahmad; scholars differ on its authenticity.
title: Sultan

name: Bayezid II
line: A quiet sultan who sent ships to rescue Muslims and Jews driven out of Spain.
story: After Granada fell in 1492, he sent the admiral Kemal Reis to carry refugees to Ottoman lands, and welcomed the Jews expelled from Spain. He built mosques and hospitals, and was forced to abdicate by his son Selim.
title: Sultan

name: Selim I
line: The grim sultan who conquered Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz and became protector of Makkah and Madinah.
story: He beat the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514, then destroyed the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq and Ridaniyya. The Sharif of Makkah sent him the keys of the holy city, and he took the title Servant of the Two Holy Sanctuaries.
title: Sultan

name: Suleiman I
line: The longest-reigning Ottoman sultan, known to Muslims as the Lawgiver.
story: He took Belgrade, Rhodes and Baghdad, won at Mohacs and besieged Vienna in 1529. He issued law codes, rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem that still stand, and his architect Sinan built the Suleymaniye Mosque. He died on campaign in Hungary.
legacy: The Ottoman state reached its classic form in his reign.
title: Sultan

name: Selim II
line: A sultan whose reign saw the conquest of Cyprus and the loss at Lepanto.
story: He left government to the vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha. Cyprus was taken in 1571 but the fleet was destroyed at Lepanto the same year. Sinan built him the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.
title: Sultan

name: Murad III
line: A sultan of long wars with Persia and Austria and rising palace intrigue.
story: He rarely left the palace. Wars with the Safavids won land in the Caucasus, and a long war with the Habsburgs began in 1593.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed III
line: The last sultan to have his brothers put to death on taking the throne.
story: On his accession nineteen brothers were killed under the old law of succession. He led his army in person and won at Keresztes in 1596.
title: Sultan

name: Ahmed I
line: The young sultan who built the Blue Mosque and ended the killing of brothers.
story: He spared his brother Mustafa, beginning the custom of the eldest male relative inheriting. He built the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, with its six minarets, facing Hagia Sophia.
title: Sultan

name: Mustafa I
line: A troubled sultan who was put on and taken off the throne twice.
story: Unfit to rule, he was deposed after three months in 1618, restored in 1622 after Osman II's murder, and removed again in 1623.
title: Sultan

name: Osman II
line: A teenage sultan killed by the Janissaries when he tried to reform them.
story: After a failed campaign in Poland he planned a new army. The Janissaries rose and killed him in 1622, the first Ottoman sultan murdered by his own soldiers.
title: Sultan

name: Murad IV
line: A stern sultan who restored order and retook Baghdad in 1638.
story: He crushed rebellions, banned tobacco, coffee and wine, and led his army in person. He retook Baghdad from the Safavids in 1638, fixing a border that roughly survives as Iraq's with Iran.
title: Sultan

name: Ibrahim
line: An unstable sultan, deposed and executed in 1648.
story: The long war for Crete with Venice began in his reign. Unpredictable and extravagant, he was deposed by officials and Janissaries and put to death.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed IV
role: Sultan of the second siege of Vienna
line: A sultan who reigned forty years, when the Koprulu viziers ran the empire and Vienna was besieged again.
story: Crowned at six, he was known as the Hunter. The Koprulu viziers restored strength and took Crete in 1669. The failed siege of Vienna in 1683 led to a long losing war, and he was deposed.
title: Sultan

name: Suleiman II
line: A sultan who spent forty years in palace confinement before a short reign of war.
story: His vizier Fazil Mustafa Koprulu won back Belgrade in 1690.
title: Sultan

name: Ahmed II
line: A brief reign marked by defeat at Slankamen.
story: His grand vizier was killed at Slankamen in 1691 against the Habsburgs.
title: Sultan

name: Mustafa II
line: The sultan whose defeat led to the Treaty of Karlowitz, the first great Ottoman loss of land.
story: He led armies himself but was crushed at Zenta in 1697. At Karlowitz in 1699 the empire gave up most of Hungary. He was deposed in a revolt in 1703.
title: Sultan

name: Ahmed III
line: A sultan of gardens and fountains, in whose reign the first Ottoman Turkish printing press opened.
story: His army trapped Peter the Great at the Pruth in 1711. The 'Tulip Era' of palaces and poetry followed, and in 1727 Ibrahim Muteferrika was allowed to print books in Turkish. A revolt deposed him in 1730.
title: Sultan

name: Mahmud I
line: A sultan who won back Belgrade and built libraries and fountains.
story: The Treaty of Belgrade in 1739 recovered lands from Austria. He founded libraries and began the Nuruosmaniye Mosque.
title: Sultan

name: Osman III
line: A short reign that completed the Nuruosmaniye Mosque.
story: Confined in the palace for fifty years before taking the throne, he ruled three years.
title: Sultan

name: Mustafa III
line: A reforming sultan whose war with Russia went badly.
story: He saw the need for military reform. In the war of 1768–1774 Russia burned the Ottoman fleet at Cesme and overran the Danube lands.
title: Sultan

name: Abdul Hamid I
line: The sultan who signed away Crimea, the first Muslim land the empire lost to Russia.
story: The Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca in 1774 freed Crimea from Ottoman rule but named the sultan caliph of its Muslims, a new use of the title. Russia annexed Crimea in 1783.
title: Sultan

name: Selim III
line: A reformer who built a modern army and was killed by those who resisted change.
story: He created the 'New Order' army and opened embassies in Europe. Napoleon invaded Egypt in his reign. The Janissaries deposed him in 1807 and he was killed the next year.
title: Sultan

name: Mustafa IV
line: A one-year sultan who ordered the deaths of Selim III and his own brother.
story: Put on the throne by the Janissaries, he had Selim killed when reformers came to restore him. He was deposed and executed.
title: Sultan

name: Mahmud II
line: The sultan who destroyed the Janissaries in 1826 and began modernising the state.
story: He waited eighteen years, then crushed the Janissary corps in 1826. He brought in a new army, new dress and the fez. Greece won independence, and his governor Muhammad Ali grew more powerful than he.
title: Sultan

name: Abdulmejid I
line: The sultan of the Tanzimat reforms, who rebuilt the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah.
story: The Gulhane edict of 1839 promised equal rights and fair taxes for all subjects. He fought Russia in the Crimean War with Britain and France. The Ottoman rebuilding of the Prophet's Mosque, much of which still stands, was done in his reign.
title: Sultan

name: Abdulaziz
line: The first sultan to visit western Europe, deposed in 1876.
story: He travelled to Paris and London in 1867 and built a large navy, but debts grew until the state went bankrupt. He was deposed and died days later.
title: Sultan

name: Murad V
line: A liberal-minded sultan who reigned only 93 days.
story: He was removed because of a breakdown and spent the rest of his life confined in a palace.
title: Sultan

name: Abdul Hamid II
line: The sultan who stressed his role as caliph of all Muslims and built the Hijaz Railway.
story: He granted a constitution in 1876 and suspended it two years later. He ruled personally for thirty years, built schools and the Hijaz Railway to Madinah, and appealed to Muslims worldwide. The Young Turks deposed him in 1909.
note: He is widely reported to have refused to sell land in Palestine to the Zionist leader Herzl.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed V
role: Sultan of the First World War
line: A sultan with little power who reigned as the empire entered the First World War.
story: The Committee of Union and Progress ruled in his name. In 1914 a call to jihad was issued in his name as caliph, but most Muslims under Allied rule did not rise.
title: Sultan

name: Mehmed VI
line: The last Ottoman sultan, who left Istanbul when the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
story: He reigned while the Allies occupied Istanbul. When the Ankara government abolished the sultanate in November 1922 he left on a British warship and died in exile in Italy.
title: Sultan

name: Abdulmejid II
line: The last Ottoman caliph, holding the title without the throne, until the caliphate was abolished in 1924.
story: When the sultanate ended, the Turkish assembly chose him as caliph only. On 3 March 1924 it abolished the caliphate and expelled the family. A painter and scholar, he died in Paris in 1944.
lesson: An office that lasted thirteen centuries ended with a vote.
title: Caliph

name: Muhammad Ali Pasha
line: An Ottoman officer from Albania who seized Egypt and remade it as a modern state.
story: He wiped out the Mamluk beys in the Citadel in 1811 and for the sultan crushed the first Saudi state, taking Diriyah in 1818. He built factories, schools and an army, and nearly toppled the Ottomans himself. His family ruled Egypt until 1952.
title: Wali

name: Emir Abd al-Qadir
line: A Sufi scholar who led Algeria's resistance to France for fifteen years.
story: Chosen emir at twenty-four, he built a state and fought the French army until 1847. After prison in France he settled in Damascus, where in 1860 he sheltered thousands of Christians from rioters. He died there in 1883.
legacy: He was honoured across the world as a man of faith, courage and mercy.
note: His state has no separate polity entry.
title: Emir

name: Imam Shamil
line: The imam of Dagestan and Chechnya who resisted the Russian Empire for twenty-five years.
story: A Naqshbandi scholar, he united the mountain peoples under Islamic law and fought Russian armies in the Caucasus forests. He surrendered at Gunib in 1859. Later allowed to make Hajj, he died in Madinah in 1871 and is buried in al-Baqi.
note: His imamate has no separate polity entry.
title: Imam

name: Muhammad ibn Saud
line: The emir of Diriyah whose pact with Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab founded the first Saudi state.
story: In 1744 he agreed to support the preaching of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. Their alliance grew into a state that later spread over much of Arabia.
note: This was the first Saudi state, long before the modern kingdom of 1932.
title: Emir

name: Abdulaziz ibn Saud
line: The founder of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, proclaimed in 1932.
story: In 1902 he retook Riyadh with a small band. Over thirty years he united Najd and the Hijaz, and in 1932 proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Oil was found in 1938.
when: Took Riyadh 1902; King of Saudi Arabia 1932–1953
title: King

name: Moulay Ismail
line: A powerful Moroccan sultan who ruled 55 years and built Meknes into an imperial city.
story: He built a vast army, won Tangier back from England in 1684 and corresponded with Louis XIV of France. His palaces and walls at Meknes are among the largest in North Africa.
title: Sultan

name: Ahmad al-Mansur
line: The Moroccan sultan who won the Battle of the Three Kings and sent an army across the Sahara.
story: He came to the throne on the day of the battle of Wadi al-Makhazin in 1578, where Portugal's king was killed. In 1591 his army destroyed Songhai at Tondibi, and Timbuktu's scholar Ahmad Baba was taken in chains to Marrakesh.
note: He ruled for the Saadi dynasty, which has no separate polity entry.
title: Sultan

name: Tipu Sultan
line: The ruler of Mysore who fought the British East India Company and died defending his capital.
story: He used rockets in battle and sought allies in France and the Ottoman court. He fought four wars against the Company and was killed at Srirangapatna in 1799.
note: The kingdom of Mysore has no separate polity entry.
title: Sultan

name: Mustafa Kemal
line: The founder of the Republic of Turkey, who abolished the sultanate and the caliphate.
story: A commander at Gallipoli, he led the war that created modern Turkey. Under his lead the assembly abolished the sultanate in 1922 and the caliphate in 1924, then closed Sufi lodges and religious courts, and changed the script to Latin letters.
note: Described here as a matter of record; Muslims judge his reforms very differently.
title: President

name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
line: The lawyer who led the movement for Pakistan and became its first governor-general.
story: Leader of the Muslim League, he argued that India's Muslims needed their own state. Pakistan was created in August 1947, and he died just over a year later.
title: Governor-General

name: Sargon of Akkad
line: The king of Akkad who built what is often called the world's first empire.
story: Legend says he was found as a baby in a basket on the river, raised by a gardener and rose to rule all of Mesopotamia. His capital Akkad has never been found.
tie: The Quran reminds its hearers of nations before them 'greater in power' who left traces in the land (30:9).
note: His dates are approximate and follow the middle chronology.
title: King

name: Hammurabi
line: The king who made Babylon great and carved one of the oldest law codes on stone.
story: He united southern Mesopotamia under Babylon and set up a stone pillar with nearly 300 laws, from trade to family life. The pillar is now in the Louvre.
tie: Babylon, the city he raised, is named in the Quran in the story of Harut and Marut (2:102).
note: Dates follow the middle chronology.
title: King

name: Ramesses II
line: The most famous pharaoh of Egypt, often suggested as the Pharaoh of Musa.
story: He reigned 66 years, fought the Hittites at Kadesh and covered Egypt with temples and giant statues, including Abu Simbel. His mummy survives in Cairo.
tie: Many modern writers link him or his son Merneptah to the Pharaoh who opposed Musa.
note: The Quran never names the Pharaoh of Musa, and scholars differ on which king he was; this identification is not certain.
title: Pharaoh

name: Ashurbanipal
line: The Assyrian king of Nineveh who gathered the greatest library of the ancient world.
story: He ruled Assyria at its height and collected thousands of clay tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh. Within twenty years of his death Nineveh was destroyed.
tie: At Ta'if the Prophet ﷺ called Nineveh 'the town of the righteous man Yunus ibn Matta' (seerah).
note: The Quran does not name the city of Yunus; tradition identifies it with Nineveh.
title: King

name: Nebuchadnezzar II
line: The Babylonian king who destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and carried Bani Israil into exile.
story: He made Babylon the greatest city of its day, with walls and famous gardens. In 587 BCE his army burned Jerusalem and the Temple of Sulayman and took its people to Babylon.
tie: Many commentators see him in the first of the two punishments of Bani Israil foretold in Surah al-Isra (17:4-5).
note: The Quran does not name him; the link to 17:4-7 comes from the commentators, who differ.
title: King

name: Cyrus the Great
line: The Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BCE and let the exiles return to Jerusalem.
story: He built the largest empire the world had yet seen. After taking Babylon he allowed deported peoples, including the Jews, to go home and rebuild their temples.
tie: Some modern Muslim scholars, such as Abul Kalam Azad, proposed that he was Dhul-Qarnayn (18:83-98).
note: Scholars differ over who Dhul-Qarnayn was. The Quran gives no name; the commentators proposed several kings, and many say the matter is best left to Allah.
title: King

name: Darius I
line: The Persian king who organised the empire and in whose reign the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt.
story: He divided the empire into provinces, built roads and the palace of Persepolis, and carved his deeds on the cliff of Behistun. The Second Temple was finished in Jerusalem around 516 BCE.
tie: The rebuilt Temple stood on the site later honoured by Muslims as the precinct of al-Masjid al-Aqsa.
title: King

name: Alexander the Great
line: The young Macedonian king who conquered Persia, Egypt and lands to the Indus.
story: Taught by Aristotle, he crossed into Asia at twenty-two, defeated Darius III, founded Alexandria in Egypt and marched to India. He died at Babylon aged thirty-two, and his empire split among his generals.
tie: Some early commentators identified him with Dhul-Qarnayn (18:83-98); others, such as Ibn Kathir, rejected this.
note: Scholars differ over who Dhul-Qarnayn was. The Quran gives no name; the commentators proposed several kings, and many say the matter is best left to Allah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyya argued that Alexander, a pagan whose minister was Aristotle, could not be the believing king of the Quran.
title: King

name: Antiochus IV
line: A Greek king who banned the law of Musa and defiled the Temple in Jerusalem.
story: In 167 BCE he forbade circumcision and the Sabbath and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. The Maccabean revolt that followed won the Jews independence for a time.
tie: His persecution is one of the trials Bani Israil faced in keeping the Torah between the prophets.
title: King

name: Aretas IV
line: The Nabataean king of Petra, in whose time the great tombs of Hegra were carved.
story: He ruled the caravan kingdom of the Nabataeans at its height, from Petra to the Hijaz. Many tombs carved into the rocks of Hegra, now al-Ula, date from his reign.
tie: Hegra lies in al-Hijr, the land of Thamud, which the Prophet ﷺ passed on the way to Tabuk (15:80-84).
note: The tombs visible today are Nabataean, centuries later than Thamud; travellers long linked them with Thamud.
title: King

name: Herod the Great
line: The Roman client king of Judea who rebuilt the Temple shortly before the birth of Isa.
story: Rome made him king of the Jews. He rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale and built fortresses such as Masada. He was known for suspicion and cruelty, even to his own family.
tie: Zakariya, Maryam and the young Isa lived in the world he ruled; the Gospels say he sought to kill the infant Isa.
note: The Quran does not mention him; the story of the infants is from the Gospel of Matthew.
title: King

name: Augustus
line: The first Roman emperor, in whose reign Isa was born.
story: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra and in 27 BCE became Augustus, ruling the Mediterranean world. His long peace let roads and trade spread.
tie: Isa ibn Maryam was born in his reign, in a province of his empire.
title: Emperor

name: Tiberius
line: The Roman emperor during the mission of Isa.
story: A gloomy and able general, he ruled from Rome and later from Capri. The town of Tiberias in Galilee was named after him.
tie: The Sea of Tiberias, named for him, appears in the hadith of Tamim al-Dari about the Dajjal.
note: The Tamim al-Dari hadith is reported by Muslim.
title: Emperor

name: Pontius Pilate
line: The Roman governor who, Christians say, ordered the crucifixion of Isa.
story: He governed Judea from Caesarea and clashed often with the Jews. The Gospels say he tried Isa and handed him over to be crucified.
tie: The Quran says they did not kill Isa nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so, and Allah raised him up (4:157-158).
title: Prefect

name: Titus
line: The Roman general who destroyed Jerusalem and the Second Temple in 70 CE.
story: Sent by his father Vespasian to crush the Jewish revolt, he besieged Jerusalem and burned the Temple in 70 CE. He later became emperor for two years.
tie: Many commentators link the Temple's second destruction with the second punishment of Bani Israil (17:7).
note: The Quran does not name him; the link comes from the commentators.
title: Emperor

name: Hadrian
line: The emperor who rebuilt Jerusalem as Aelia, the source of its Arabic name Iliya.
story: After a Jewish revolt he refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from living there.
tie: Aelia became 'Iliya', the name used for Jerusalem in the hadith of Heraclius and in Umar's treaty.
title: Emperor

name: Decius
line: The emperor the commentators name as the king the People of the Cave fled.
story: He ordered all subjects to sacrifice to the Roman gods in 250, the first empire-wide persecution of Christians. Christian legend tells of seven youths of Ephesus who hid in a cave and slept for centuries.
tie: Commentators call the tyrant of the Cave story Daqyanus, a name drawn from this legend (18:9-26).
note: The name comes from the commentators, not the Quran, which names neither king nor city.
title: Emperor

name: Theodosius II
line: The emperor in whose reign, the legend says, the sleepers of the cave awoke.
story: He built the great land walls of Constantinople, which held for a thousand years, and issued a famous law code.
tie: In the Christian telling of the Cave story, the youths wake under this believing emperor (18:19-21).
note: The link comes from legend and the commentators, not the Quran.
title: Emperor

name: Constantine
line: The Roman emperor who embraced Christianity, called the Council of Nicaea and founded Constantinople.
story: He gave Christians freedom in 313 and called the Council of Nicaea in 325, which declared Isa to be of one substance with God. In 330 he made Byzantium his new capital, Constantinople.
tie: The Quran calls Christians back from the Trinity to the pure oneness of Allah (4:171).
title: Emperor

name: Ezana
line: The king of Aksum who made his kingdom one of the first Christian states.
story: His coins changed from the crescent and disc to the cross. Aksum traded with Rome, Arabia and India.
tie: Three centuries later a Christian king of Aksum sheltered the first Muslim emigrants.
title: King

name: Kaleb
line: The Aksumite king who invaded Yemen after the burning of the Christians of Najran.
story: In about 525 he sent an army across the Red Sea, defeated Dhu Nuwas and took Yemen. Abraha, a commander of that army, later made himself ruler there.
tie: The Quran curses 'the companions of the trench' (85:4); commentators tie this to Dhu Nuwas and Najran.
title: King

name: Justinian
line: The Byzantine emperor who built Hagia Sophia and codified Roman law.
story: He reconquered Italy and North Africa, collected Roman law into one code and rebuilt Hagia Sophia in 537, the largest church in the world for centuries.
tie: Hagia Sophia became a mosque when Mehmed II took the city in 1453.
title: Emperor

name: Khosrow I
line: The Persian king in whose reign the Prophet ﷺ was born.
story: He reformed taxes, built the great arch of Ctesiphon and welcomed philosophers. Late in his reign Persian forces took Yemen from the Aksumites.
tie: The Prophet ﷺ was born in his reign, around 570.
note: A saying that the Prophet ﷺ was glad to be born 'in the time of the just king' is judged baseless by hadith scholars.
title: King

name: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan
line: A Yemeni prince who drove the Abyssinians out of Yemen with Persian help.
