story: After Abraha's line ruled Yemen, he sought help from Khosrow I, who sent a small force. They expelled the Abyssinians, and Sayf ruled as a Persian vassal until he was killed.
tie: Seerah books say Abd al-Muttalib led a delegation to congratulate him and heard a prophecy of the coming prophet.
note: The report of Abd al-Muttalib's visit and the prophecy is weak.
title: King

name: Al-Numan ibn al-Mundhir
line: The last Arab king of al-Hira, whose death led to the Battle of Dhi Qar.
story: A patron of Arab poets, he ruled for Persia on the desert frontier. Khosrow II had him killed, and the Arab tribes later beat a Persian army at Dhi Qar.
tie: Dhi Qar showed Arabs, in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, that Persia could be beaten.
note: A report that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of Dhi Qar as the first day the Arabs won justice from Persia has a disputed chain.
title: King

name: Heraclius
line: The Byzantine emperor who received the Prophet's ﷺ letter and questioned Abu Sufyan about him.
story: He took the throne as Persia overran the empire, then turned the war around and won by 628. That year the Prophet's ﷺ letter reached him, and he questioned Abu Sufyan closely about the Prophet. He did not accept Islam, and lost Syria at Yarmuk in 636.
tie: The Quran foretold that the defeated Romans would soon be victorious (30:2-4).
title: Emperor

name: Khosrow II
role: Sasanian king who tore the letter
line: The Persian emperor who tore up the Prophet's ﷺ letter, and whose empire soon fell apart.
story: He conquered Jerusalem and Egypt from Byzantium, but Heraclius struck back into Persia. When the Prophet's ﷺ letter reached him he tore it, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed that his kingdom be torn apart. He was killed by his own son in 628.
tie: His victory over the Romans is the defeat mentioned at the opening of Surah al-Rum (30:2-4).
title: King

name: Yazdegerd III
line: The last king of Persia, who fled east after Qadisiyyah and Nahavand.
story: Crowned as a boy, he saw his armies lost at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand. He fled from city to city and was killed near Merv in 651.
tie: The fall of his empire fulfilled the Prophet's ﷺ words that the treasures of Kisra would be spent in Allah's way.
note: The saying about Kisra's treasures is in the Sahih collections.
title: King

name: Al-Muqawqis
line: The ruler of Egypt who answered the Prophet's ﷺ letter politely and sent gifts, including Mariyah.
story: He received the Prophet's ﷺ letter, wrote a courteous reply and sent gifts: two Coptic women, Mariyah and Sirin, a mule and cloth. He did not accept Islam. Egypt was won by Amr ibn al-As in the 640s.
tie: Mariyah, sent by him, became the mother of the Prophet's ﷺ son Ibrahim.
note: His identity is uncertain; he is often identified with Cyrus, the Patriarch of Alexandria, but dates do not fit perfectly.
title: Governor

name: Jabalah ibn al-Ayham
line: The last Ghassanid king, who became Muslim but left over a ruling of Umar.
story: The Ghassanids were Christian Arab allies of Byzantium. The histories say Jabalah accepted Islam, but when Umar ordered him to face retaliation for striking a Bedouin during tawaf, he fled to Byzantium.
tie: His story is told to show that, under Umar, a king and a Bedouin were equal before the law.
note: The story is famous in the histories, but its chain is not strong.
title: King

name: Constans II
line: The Byzantine emperor defeated by the first Muslim navy at the Battle of the Masts in 655.
story: He lost Egypt and much of North Africa. In 655 his fleet met the new Muslim navy off Lycia at Dhat al-Sawari and was routed; he barely escaped.
tie: The battle showed that Muslims, a desert people, had become a sea power.
title: Emperor

name: Leo III the Isaurian
line: The Byzantine emperor who held Constantinople against the great Muslim siege of 717–718.
story: He seized the throne just as Maslamah's army and fleet arrived. Walls, Greek fire and a harsh winter broke the siege. He later banned religious images, starting the Iconoclast controversy.
tie: Some historians think the Muslim rejection of images influenced his iconoclasm; others disagree.
title: Emperor

name: Charles Martel
line: The Frankish leader who stopped the Muslim army at Tours in 732.
story: He ruled the Franks in the name of puppet kings. Near Tours in 732 his infantry held against the army of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who was killed; Arab historians called it the Court of the Martyrs.
tie: Tours marked the northern limit of Muslim expansion in western Europe.
title: Mayor of the Palace

name: Charlemagne
line: The Frankish emperor who exchanged embassies and gifts with Harun al-Rashid.
story: He united much of western Europe and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. He fought in Spain, where his rearguard was destroyed at Roncevaux in 778. Harun al-Rashid sent him an elephant named Abul-Abbas.
tie: His embassies with Baghdad show how far the Abbasid name carried in Europe.
note: The embassies are known from Frankish sources; Arabic sources do not mention them.
title: Emperor

name: Nikephoros I
line: The emperor who refused Harun's tribute and received his famous one-line reply.
story: He wrote demanding back the tribute paid by the empress Irene. Al-Tabari reports Harun's reply: 'The answer is what you will see, not what you will hear.' Harun then took Heraclea in 806, and Nikephoros paid again.
tie: The exchange became a model of the confident early caliphate.
title: Emperor

name: Romanos IV Diogenes
line: The Byzantine emperor captured by Alp Arslan at Manzikert in 1071.
story: Betrayed by part of his army, he was taken prisoner. Alp Arslan treated him as a guest and freed him for a ransom, but at home rivals blinded him and he died soon after.
tie: The sultan's mercy to him was remembered in both Muslim and Byzantine accounts.
title: Emperor

name: Alexios I Komnenos
role: Emperor who called for the Crusade
line: The Byzantine emperor whose appeal for help led to the First Crusade.
story: After Manzikert he asked the Pope for soldiers against the Turks. The Pope's call in 1095 brought far larger armies than he wanted, which went on to take Jerusalem.
tie: The Crusades that followed shaped relations between Islam and Europe for two centuries.
title: Emperor

name: Alfonso VI
line: The Castilian king who took Toledo in 1085 and was beaten at Zallaqa the next year.
story: He forced the taifa kings to pay him tribute and in 1085 took Toledo, the old Visigothic capital. Alarmed, the taifas called in the Almoravids, who defeated him at Zallaqa in 1086.
tie: He styled himself 'emperor of the two religions', ruling Christians and Muslims.
title: King
wiki: Alfonso VI of León and Castile

name: Roger II of Sicily
line: The Norman king of Sicily whose court was half Arab and who commissioned al-Idrisi's world map.
story: He ruled from Palermo with Muslim officials and soldiers and wore robes with Arabic writing. The geographer al-Idrisi made for him a great silver map and the book known as the Book of Roger.
tie: His court carried Islamic learning from Sicily into Europe.
note: Norman Sicily has no separate polity entry.
title: King

name: Baldwin I
line: The first Crusader to take the title King of Jerusalem.
story: He first seized Edessa, then after his brother Godfrey's death was crowned in Jerusalem, a year after the Crusaders' massacre of its people. He took most of the coastal cities.
tie: For 88 years al-Aqsa was in Crusader hands, until Salah al-Din returned.
title: King

name: Guy of Lusignan
line: The Crusader king captured at Hattin, to whom Salah al-Din offered water.
story: He led the Crusader army into the waterless hills near Hattin in 1187. Captured, he was offered a cup of iced water by Salah al-Din, who told him, 'Kings do not kill kings', but killed Reynald.
tie: His capture opened the road for Salah al-Din to Jerusalem.
title: King

name: Richard I
role: King of England on the Third Crusade
line: The Lionheart, who fought Salah al-Din but never took Jerusalem.
story: He took Acre in 1191 and had about 2,700 Muslim prisoners killed. He won at Arsuf but turned back short of Jerusalem. In 1192 he made a truce with Salah al-Din letting pilgrims visit the city.
tie: His rivalry with Salah al-Din became a legend of mutual respect in both Europe and the Muslim world.
title: King

name: Frederick II
line: The Arabic-speaking emperor who won Jerusalem by treaty, not battle, in 1229.
story: Raised in Sicily, he spoke Arabic and kept Muslim soldiers at Lucera. Excommunicated by the Pope, he sailed east and in 1229 agreed with al-Kamil to receive Jerusalem for ten years.
tie: His treaty showed that Jerusalem could change hands by agreement, to the anger of both sides.
title: Emperor

name: Louis IX
line: The French king captured in Egypt in 1250 who died outside Tunis on a second crusade.
story: He invaded Egypt in 1249, took Damietta, but was defeated and captured near al-Mansurah and ransomed. In 1270 he landed at Tunis and died of disease in camp.
tie: His defeat in Egypt brought the Mamluks to power.
note: Arabs called all western Crusaders 'Franks', so he is placed with the Franks here.
title: King

name: Genghis Khan
line: The Mongol conqueror whose armies destroyed the great cities of the eastern Muslim world.
story: He united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and built the largest land empire in history. After the Khwarazm Shah killed his envoys, his armies laid waste to Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and Nishapur from 1219, killing vast numbers.
tie: Within three generations his descendants in Iran, Russia and Central Asia had become Muslims.
note: Juvayni reports that he told the people of Bukhara he was 'the punishment of God'. Death tolls are uncertain.
title: Khan

name: Constantine XI
line: The last Byzantine emperor, who died defending Constantinople in 1453.
story: With a few thousand men he held the walls against Mehmed II for seven weeks. When the city fell on 29 May 1453, he died fighting.
tie: His fall ended the Roman empire whose emperor Heraclius had received the Prophet's ﷺ letter.
title: Emperor

name: Ferdinand II of Aragon
line: The king who, with Isabella, conquered Granada in 1492, ending Muslim rule in Spain.
story: His marriage to Isabella joined Aragon and Castile. Together they took Granada in 1492 under a treaty that protected Muslim worship; within ten years Muslims were forced to convert or leave.
tie: The broken treaty of Granada led to the forced conversions of the Moriscos and their final expulsion in 1609.
title: King

name: Isabella I of Castile
line: The queen of Castile who took Granada, expelled Spain's Jews and sponsored Columbus in 1492.
story: With Ferdinand she finished the conquest of Granada in January 1492. That year she ordered Jews to convert or leave and funded Columbus's voyage. Forced baptisms of Muslims began in 1499.
tie: The Inquisition she backed hunted Muslims and Jews who kept their faith in secret.
title: Queen

name: Ivan IV
line: Ivan the Terrible, the first tsar, who conquered the Muslim khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan.
story: He took Kazan in 1552 after a bloody siege and Astrakhan in 1556, opening the Volga to Russia. St Basil's Cathedral in Moscow celebrates the fall of Kazan.
tie: Kazan's Tatars, Muslim since the Volga Bulgars accepted Islam in 922, came under Russian rule.
title: Tsar

name: Catherine the Great
line: The Russian empress who annexed Crimea and set up an official body for Russia's Muslims.
story: Her wars with the Ottomans won the Black Sea coast, and in 1783 she annexed Crimea. She allowed mosques to be built and in 1788 created the Orenburg Muslim Spiritual Assembly. A Quran was printed in St Petersburg in 1787.
tie: Crimea was the first Muslim-majority land the Ottomans lost to a Christian power.
title: Empress

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
line: The French general who invaded Egypt in 1798 and later became emperor.
story: He landed at Alexandria in 1798, beat the Mamluks at the Pyramids and claimed to respect Islam. Cairo rose against him and his guns shelled al-Azhar. He left in 1799, seized power in France and was crowned emperor in 1804.
tie: His invasion woke the Muslim world to Europe's new power; al-Jabarti recorded it from Cairo.
title: Emperor

name: Queen Victoria
role: Queen of Britain, Empress of India
line: The British queen who ruled over more Muslims than any other monarch of her time.
story: After 1857 the British Crown took India from the East India Company, and in 1876 she became Empress of India. Her empire held Muslims from Egypt to Malaya. Late in life she learned Urdu from her Indian Muslim secretary, Abdul Karim.
tie: Her reign marked the height of European rule over Muslim lands.
title: Queen

name: Ur-Nammu
line: The king of Ur who built its great ziggurat and wrote one of the oldest law codes.
story: He founded the Third Dynasty of Ur, raised a stepped temple to the moon god Nanna and set down laws with fines for crimes, three centuries before Hammurabi.
tie: Tradition places Ibrahim's early life in Ur, a city of moon and star worship like the one he rejected (6:76-79).
note: Linking Ibrahim's homeland to this Ur is a later tradition; scholars differ.
title: King

name: Akhenaten
line: The pharaoh who closed Egypt's temples and ordered worship of the sun-disc alone.
story: He built a new capital at Amarna for the Aten. After his death his city was abandoned and his name was struck from the monuments.
tie: His sun cult is sometimes called early monotheism, but the Quran forbids bowing to the sun, its Creator alone is worshipped (41:37).
title: Pharaoh

name: Merneptah
line: Ramesses II's son, whose victory stone is the oldest mention of Israel outside scripture.
story: He came to the throne old, after his father's long reign, and fought Libyans and the Sea Peoples. His stele names a people called Israel in Canaan.
tie: Some writers identify him with the Pharaoh of the Exodus; others prefer his father or an earlier king.
note: The Quran does not name the Pharaoh of Musa; any identification is uncertain.
title: Pharaoh

name: Sargon II
line: The Assyrian king who completed the conquest of Samaria and deported the northern tribes of Israel.
story: He finished the siege of Samaria and scattered its people across his empire, and built a new capital at Dur-Sharrukin. He died in battle.
tie: The scattering of the tribes was one of the trials of Bani Israil that the Quran recalls (7:168).
title: King

name: Julius Caesar
line: The Roman general who set the solar calendar of 365 days and was murdered in 44 BCE.
story: He conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon and made himself dictator. His calendar, with a leap year, was later refined into the one most of the world uses today.
tie: The Quran fixes the year at twelve lunar months (9:36); Muslims keep the Hijri calendar beside his solar one.
title: Dictator

name: Shapur I
line: The Persian king who captured the Roman emperor Valerian in 260.
story: He beat three Roman emperors and carved the scene of Valerian kneeling before him in the rock at Naqsh-e Rostam.
tie: The long Roman-Persian wars he fought had exhausted both empires by the time of the Prophet ﷺ.
title: King

name: Valerian
line: The only Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.
story: He persecuted Christians, then marched east and was captured by Shapur I near Edessa in 260. He died in captivity.
tie: Rome and Persia, the two powers of the Prophet's ﷺ letters, were already locked in war in his time.
title: Emperor

name: Imru' al-Qays ibn Amr
line: An early Lakhmid king whose tomb carries one of the oldest inscriptions in the Arabic language.
story: His epitaph at al-Namara in the Syrian desert, dated 328, calls him 'king of all the Arabs'. It is written in Arabic words with Nabataean letters.
tie: The inscription shows the Arabic language of the Quran taking written shape three centuries before revelation.
title: King

name: Theodosius I
role: Emperor who made Christianity the state faith
line: The emperor who made Nicene Christianity the one lawful religion of Rome.
story: His edict of 380 declared the Nicene creed the faith of the empire, and in the 390s he banned pagan sacrifice. He was the last emperor to rule both east and west.
tie: The creed he enforced, of Isa as divine, is what the Quran calls Christians to leave (5:72-75).
title: Emperor

name: Pelayo
line: The Visigothic noble whose small victory at Covadonga began the Christian kingdoms of the north.
story: Refusing Muslim rule, he held out in the Asturian mountains and beat a small force at Covadonga. Arab chroniclers dismissed his band as thirty men, but his kingdom grew.
tie: Spanish memory counts Covadonga as the start of the 'Reconquista' that ended al-Andalus.
title: King

name: Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik
line: The Umayyad prince who led the great siege of Constantinople in 717–718.
story: A son of Abd al-Malik, he spent his life on the Byzantine and Caucasus fronts. His army besieged Constantinople for a year until hunger, cold and Greek fire forced Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz to call it home.
note: He never ruled as caliph; his dates are those of his main commands.
title: Prince

name: Roger I of Sicily
line: The Norman knight who conquered Muslim Sicily over thirty years.
story: With his brother Robert Guiscard he took Palermo in 1072, and the last Muslim town fell in 1091. He kept Muslim soldiers and officials in his service.
tie: His conquest ended Muslim rule in Sicily, begun by the Aghlabids in 827.
note: Norman Sicily has no separate polity entry.
title: Count

name: Hummay
line: The king of Kanem near Lake Chad who accepted Islam in the 11th century.
story: Chronicles say a scholar named Muhammad ibn Mani taught him the Quran. Kanem, and later Bornu, remained a Muslim kingdom for some eight centuries.
title: Mai

name: Sultan Hasan
line: A son of al-Nasir Muhammad who built one of the largest mosques in Cairo.
story: He reigned twice, in the years of the Black Death. His vast mosque-college below the Citadel taught all four Sunni schools. He was killed by his own emirs in 1361.
title: Sultan

name: Philip III of Spain
line: The Spanish king who expelled the Moriscos from 1609, ending nine centuries of Islam in Spain.
story: His government ordered out the descendants of Muslims who had been forced to convert. About 300,000 were shipped to North Africa between 1609 and 1614.
tie: With the Moriscos gone, the last Muslims of al-Andalus vanished from Spain.
title: King

name: Muhammad Ahmad
line: A Sudanese Sufi who declared himself the Mahdi in 1881 and took Khartoum from the British-backed Egyptians.
story: He gathered followers against corrupt Egyptian rule, won battle after battle and took Khartoum in 1885, where General Gordon was killed. He died months later; his successor ruled until 1898.
note: Most scholars rejected his claim to be the Mahdi. His state has no separate polity entry.
title: Imam
